tests.result: The ABS module (EBCM) stores C0035 as a history code with multiple occurrences; the scan tool's enhanced ABS menu describes it as a left front wheel speed sensor circuit fault. The snapshot shows the LF wheel speed at 0 while the other three read about 52 km/h.
tests.teaches: Chassis codes are often manufacturer-specific, so use the scan tool's enhanced description and OEM service information for the exact meaning. The snapshot shows one wheel dropping to zero while the others kept reading, which points at that wheel's sensor circuit.

tests.title: Graph all four wheel speeds on a road test
tests.result: With a helper recording data on a rough road, the LF wheel speed drops to zero for a fraction of a second over bumps, then returns to match the others. On smooth pavement all four wheels track together.
tests.teaches: A signal that drops out completely and instantly, and only over bumps, suggests an intermittent open circuit. A weak sensor or damaged tone ring more often produces erratic or low readings.

tests.title: Wiggle test the LF sensor circuit while monitoring continuity
tests.result: With the truck on a lift and the wheels hanging, a meter monitoring continuity between the EBCM connector and the sensor connector (terminals identified from the OEM wiring diagram) shows one circuit going open intermittently when the harness is flexed near the upper control arm.
tests.teaches: Intermittent opens need a test that runs while you move the harness. Monitoring continuity or live data during a wiggle test finds the exact spot where the circuit breaks. Safety: support the vehicle properly and keep hands clear of suspension pinch points.

tests.title: Trace and inspect the LF sensor harness along the suspension
tests.result: The harness is missing one retaining clip and rests against the upper control arm. At that spot the jacket is worn through, and one conductor is broken inside the insulation; the ends separate as the suspension moves.
tests.teaches: Wheel speed sensor harnesses move with the suspension and steering. When a clip is left off after repair work, the harness can rub through. Inspecting routing and retainers along the whole path finds the cause, not just the break.

tests.title: Check the sensor signal at the sensor connector while spinning the wheel
tests.result: With a breakout lead at the sensor connector and the wheel spun by hand, the sensor produces a clean, consistent signal as long as the harness is not flexed.
tests.teaches: Testing the signal at the sensor connector separates the sensor from the wiring. A good signal at the sensor with a dropout at the module means the fault is in the harness between them. Identify the sensor type (active or passive) from OEM service information before testing.

tests.title: Measure the wheel speed sensor resistance
tests.result: The meter shows a reading, but in this scenario the sensor is an active (powered) type, and OEM service information does not use resistance to test it. The reading tells you little.
tests.teaches: Resistance tests apply to passive (magnetic) sensors. Active sensors are tested for supply, ground, and signal per the OEM procedure. Always identify the sensor type first.

tests.title: Check wheel bearing play and tone ring condition
tests.result: The hub bearing has no noticeable play or noise, and the consistent signal at the sensor indicates the integrated tone ring is intact.
tests.teaches: Excess bearing play or a damaged tone ring can cause wheel speed faults, usually as erratic readings. It is a reasonable check, but it does not fit a signal that drops to zero only when the harness moves.

tests.title: Replace the LF hub bearing and sensor assembly
tests.result: The new hub assembly is installed, and the ABS light returns on the next rough road because the harness damage was not addressed.
tests.teaches: Where the sensor is part of the hub, replacing the sensor means an expensive hub replacement. Test the circuit before replacing the hub, especially after previous work in the area.

tests.title: Replace the ABS module (EBCM)
tests.result: After the module is replaced and programmed, the LF wheel speed still drops out over bumps, and C0035 returns.
tests.teaches: The module correctly reported a real circuit fault. Module replacement is costly and requires programming, and it is rarely justified when one wheel circuit has a fault.

tests.title: Clear the ABS codes and return the vehicle
tests.result: The light goes out, then comes back on the next rough road.
tests.teaches: An intermittent fault will return. Clearing codes without a repair solves nothing, and the customer loses ABS and traction control whenever the fault is active.

tests.title: Bleed the brakes
tests.result: The brake fluid is refreshed, and the ABS light still comes on over bumps.
tests.teaches: Bleeding addresses hydraulic concerns, not an electrical sensor circuit fault. It does not fit the evidence.

scenarios.debrief: The ABS light is a messenger. The EBCM stored C0035, which the scan tool described as a left front wheel speed sensor circuit fault, and that tells you which circuit to test, not which part to replace. The snapshot and a recorded road test showed the LF wheel speed dropping instantly to zero over bumps and recovering while the other wheels kept reading. A clean drop to zero points to an intermittent open, not a weak sensor or damaged tone ring, which usually produce erratic or low readings. The customer's mention of a hub replacement last year was a useful clue, because work in that area can leave a harness mis-routed or missing a clip. With the truck supported and the wheel hanging, a wiggle test while monitoring the circuit found an open when the harness flexed near the upper control arm, and a visual trace found the chafed section and the missing clip. Checking the signal at the sensor connector confirmed the sensor itself worked. On this design, replacing the sensor means replacing the hub, an expensive guess. Repair the conductors per OEM wiring repair guidance, restore the routing and clips, clear the codes, and verify with a rough-road test.
commonMistakes: Replacing the hub and sensor assembly without testing the circuit.
Using a resistance test on an active wheel speed sensor without checking the OEM test procedure.
Repairing the broken wire without restoring the harness routing and clips, so it chafes through again.

scenarios.title: Pulsating brake pedal
scenarios.complaint: Brake pedal pulsation and steering wheel shimmy when braking from highway speed.
scenarios.customerStatement: When I brake coming off the highway, the pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes. It started a few thousand miles after I got new tires at a tire shop. The brakes were done about a year ago.
scenarios.rootCause: Excessive front rotor lateral runout caused by rust scale on the hub mounting faces and uneven, impact-gun lug nut torque, which led to rotor thickness variation.

tests.title: Road test to confirm the pulsation and where it is felt
tests.result: Moderate braking from highway speed produces a pedal pulsation and a steering wheel shimmy. Light braking at low speed is smoother, and there is no pull to either side.
tests.teaches: Confirming the complaint and noting where it is felt matters: a steering wheel shimmy usually points to the front brakes, while a pulsation felt only in the seat or pedal can point to the rear. Road test safely and legally.

tests.title: Check lug nut torque with a torque wrench
tests.result: Checking each lug nut with a torque wrench set to the OEM specification shows uneven tightening on both front wheels: several nuts are far tighter than the others, consistent with an impact gun.
tests.teaches: Uneven or excessive lug nut torque can distort the rotor hat and create lateral runout. It is a quick check and a strong clue, especially after recent tire work. Always use the OEM specification and a star pattern.

tests.title: Measure rotor lateral runout on the vehicle with a dial indicator
tests.result: With the rotors clamped by lug nuts torqued to specification in a star pattern, the dial indicator shows about 0.004 in (0.10 mm) of runout on the left front rotor; in this scenario both front rotors exceed the limit in the service information.
tests.teaches: Lateral runout is measured with a dial indicator on the rotor face, with the rotor clamped at the correct torque. Excess runout makes the rotor brush the pads once per revolution, wearing thickness variation into it over time. Compare readings with the OEM specification.

tests.title: Measure rotor thickness variation with a micrometer
tests.result: Measurements at several points around each front rotor show thickness variation beyond the OEM limit: a small amount, but enough to be felt in the pedal. Neither rotor is below minimum thickness.
tests.teaches: Thickness variation is what the driver feels as pedal pulsation; runout is usually what creates it. Measuring both explains the symptom and its cause. Also compare against the minimum thickness marked on the rotor.

tests.title: Remove the rotor, then inspect and measure hub flange runout
tests.result: With the rotor removed, the hub face has uneven rust scale. After cleaning with a hub-resurfacing tool, hub flange runout measured with the dial indicator is within the OEM limit, and the bearing has no play.
tests.teaches: Rust between the hub and the rotor hat tilts the rotor and adds runout. Measuring the hub separates a hub or bearing problem from a mounting-surface problem, and a clean hub face is essential before installing any rotor.

tests.title: Inspect the pads, caliper slides, and pad material transfer
tests.result: The pads have adequate thickness and even wear, the slides move freely, and there is some uneven pad material deposit on the rotor faces.
tests.teaches: Sticking slides and uneven pad deposits can contribute to pulsation, so this is a reasonable check. It does not explain the measured runout.

tests.title: Check the front suspension and steering components
tests.result: There is no looseness in the ball joints, tie rod ends, or control arm bushings.
tests.teaches: Worn suspension parts can amplify a brake shimmy, but they do not cause pedal pulsation. Worth a look, low yield.

tests.title: Balance the front wheels
tests.result: The wheels are within balance, and the shimmy occurs only while braking, not while cruising.
tests.teaches: Imbalance causes vibration at certain speeds whether or not you are braking. A vibration that appears only under braking points to the brakes.

tests.title: Resurface the rotors on an off-car lathe and reinstall
tests.result: The rotors are now flat and parallel, but after they are reinstalled on the uncleaned hubs, measured runout is still excessive.
tests.teaches: Machining removes thickness variation from the rotor but does not fix the mounting problem. Without cleaning the hub face and measuring runout after installation, the pulsation comes back.

tests.title: Replace the front rotors and pads without measuring
tests.result: The pedal is smooth for a few thousand miles, then the pulsation returns because the rusty hub faces and uneven lug nut torque were never addressed.
tests.teaches: New rotors on rusty hubs with impact-gun torque develop runout and thickness variation again. Fix the cause: clean the hub faces, check runout after installation, and torque lug nuts to the OEM specification in a star pattern.

tests.title: Replace the front calipers
tests.result: The new calipers do not change the pulsation.
tests.teaches: The calipers were not sticking, and calipers do not cause lateral runout. Replacing working hydraulic parts adds cost and risk without addressing the cause.

scenarios.debrief: Brake pulsation is almost always felt as rotor thickness variation, but the real question is what created it. The timing mattered here: the pulsation began a few thousand miles after new tires, which points toward how the wheels were installed rather than toward the brake parts themselves. The road test confirmed a pedal pulsation with steering shimmy, pointing to the front brakes. Checking lug nut torque before removal found uneven, impact-gun tightening. With the rotors properly clamped, a dial indicator showed lateral runout beyond the OEM limit, and a micrometer found thickness variation developing. Runout makes the rotor brush the pads once per revolution, wearing uneven spots that the driver eventually feels. Removing the rotor revealed rust scale on the hub face; after cleaning, the hub itself measured within the limit and the bearing had no play. The fix is not just parts: clean the hub faces, resurface or replace the rotors as the measurements dictate, re-measure runout after installation (indexing the rotor or using correction methods if needed), and torque the lug nuts to the OEM specification in a star pattern with a torque wrench. Replacing rotors without addressing the hubs and torque brings the pulsation back.
commonMistakes: Replacing rotors and pads without measuring runout or cleaning the hub faces.
Tightening lug nuts with an impact gun instead of a torque wrench set to the OEM specification in a star pattern.
Measuring runout with the rotor loose on the hub instead of clamped at the correct torque.

scenarios.title: A/C blowing warm
scenarios.complaint: A/C blows warm air at all speeds.
scenarios.customerStatement: The air conditioning stopped cooling a few days ago. It just blows warm, even on the highway. My neighbor said to buy a can of refrigerant and top it off, but I wanted someone to look at it first.
scenarios.rootCause: Open A/C compressor clutch coil winding. The PCM commands the clutch relay, and power and ground reach the coil connector, but the coil draws no current, so the clutch never engages. The refrigerant charge and the compressor itself were not the fault.

tests.title: Verify the complaint by measuring vent temperature
tests.result: With the A/C on maximum, recirculation selected, and the engine at 1500 RPM, the center vent blows air at about the same temperature as the outside air.
tests.teaches: Verifying the complaint is required and gives you a baseline for checking the repair, but it does not discriminate between causes.

tests.title: Watch whether the compressor clutch engages
tests.result: With the engine running and the A/C commanded on, the compressor pulley spins but the clutch hub stays stationary, and there is no click when the A/C is switched on.
tests.teaches: A clutch that never engages means the compressor is not pumping at all, which explains the warm air. The next question is whether the system chose not to engage it or could not. Safety: keep hands, tools, and clothing clear of the belt and pulleys.

tests.title: Check A/C request, clutch relay command, and A/C pressure sensor data
tests.result: With the A/C selected, the scan tool shows A/C request YES and clutch relay command ON, and the A/C pressure sensor reading is plausible and steady. No HVAC or engine codes are stored.
tests.teaches: Scan data tells you whether the control system is asking for the compressor. An active command and a plausible pressure reading mean the PCM is not locking out the compressor for low pressure or a sensor fault, which moves the focus to the clutch circuit.

tests.title: Read static and running pressure patterns with manifold gauges (EPA 609 certified technician)
tests.result: Engine off, both gauges read the same static pressure, consistent with the pressure-temperature chart for today's ambient temperature, so refrigerant is present. Engine running with the A/C commanded on, the low side never pulls down and the high side never climbs; both stay near static pressure, so no pressure split develops.
tests.teaches: Static pressure only shows that some refrigerant is present; it cannot tell you how much. The charge amount is verified only by recovering and weighing the refrigerant against the OEM specification. Running pressures that never split mean the compressor is not pumping. Under EPA Section 609, technicians who service motor vehicle A/C for compensation must be certified and use approved equipment; wear eye protection and gloves, and never vent refrigerant.

tests.title: Check the A/C clutch fuse and relay
tests.result: The A/C clutch fuse is intact. The relay clicks when commanded and passes battery voltage to its output under a test-light load.
tests.teaches: The fuse and relay are quick checks in the clutch feed path. Both pass, which pushes the fault further toward the clutch.

tests.title: Check power and ground at the clutch coil connector while commanded on
tests.result: Backprobing the clutch connector with the A/C commanded on shows battery voltage on the feed and a good ground with low voltage drop. Power and ground reach the coil, but the clutch does not engage.
tests.teaches: Power and ground present at a load that does not work points to the load itself. This is the test that separates the clutch coil from everything upstream of it.

tests.title: Measure clutch coil resistance with the connector unplugged
tests.result: With the connector unplugged, the meter reads OL (open) across the clutch coil. The normal value for this coil is found in OEM service information, but an open reading is a failure on any coil.
tests.teaches: An open coil cannot create the magnetic field that pulls the clutch in. Combined with power and ground present at the connector, an open coil confirms the diagnosis.

tests.title: Measure the clutch air gap
tests.result: The air gap measured with feeler gauges is within the OEM specification.
tests.teaches: An excessive air gap can keep a clutch from engaging, especially when hot, so it is a sensible check on a clutch that will not pull in. It passes here, which keeps the coil as the prime suspect.

tests.title: Add refrigerant from a can to top off the system
tests.result: The pressure readings rise, but the clutch still does not engage and the air stays warm. The system is now at risk of being overcharged, and the actual charge amount is unknown.
tests.teaches: Adding refrigerant without a verified diagnosis is guesswork, and overcharging can damage components. The charge is verified only by recovering and weighing the refrigerant, then charging to the OEM specification on the underhood label or in service information. Refrigerant service requires EPA Section 609 certification, and venting refrigerant is prohibited.

tests.title: Replace the A/C compressor
tests.result: The new compressor, which comes with a new clutch, works, but the customer paid for a complete compressor plus refrigerant recovery, evacuation, and recharge when the coil was the only fault.
tests.teaches: When a compressor will not engage, confirm why before replacing it. On many compressors the clutch or coil is serviceable separately; check OEM service information. Replacing the whole compressor is costly, requires refrigerant recovery by a Section 609 certified technician, and may be unnecessary.

tests.title: Replace the A/C pressure sensor
tests.result: The new sensor reads the same values as the old one, and the clutch still does not engage.
tests.teaches: The pressure sensor reading was already plausible, and the PCM was commanding the clutch on. A sensor that reports correctly should not be replaced.

scenarios.debrief: Warm air from the A/C has three broad causes: the compressor is not running, the refrigerant charge or flow is wrong, or air is being mixed or routed wrong inside the HVAC case. The fastest first look is the clutch: the pulley spun but the clutch hub stayed still, so the compressor was not pumping at all. The next question is whether the system chose not to engage it or could not. Scan data showed an A/C request, an active clutch relay command, and a plausible pressure sensor reading, so the PCM was not locking out the compressor. Gauges connected by an EPA Section 609 certified technician showed equal static pressures matching the pressure-temperature chart, so refrigerant was present, and no pressure split with the engine running, which fits a compressor that is not turning. Static pressure never tells you the charge amount; only recovering and weighing does. With power and ground confirmed at the clutch connector, the open coil reading proved the coil could not pull in the clutch. Adding refrigerant would have risked an overcharge and fixed nothing. Repair per OEM service information, then verify clutch engagement, a normal pressure split, and cold vent air.
commonMistakes: Adding refrigerant from a can without diagnosing, which can overcharge the system and leaves the real fault in place.
Assuming static pressure tells you the refrigerant charge amount; only recovering and weighing the charge does.
Replacing the compressor without checking power, ground, and the clutch coil.
Connecting gauges or handling refrigerant without EPA Section 609 certification and approved equipment.
